authorization: Product owner authorized creation of one dedicated private R2 bucket named insite-backups, and explicitly withheld authorization for API-token creation until the bucket exists and has been inspected.
method: Cloudflare console, product owner's authenticated session. One bucket created. Nothing else created, enabled, modified or deleted.

bucketCreation.name: insite-backups
bucketCreation.locationChoice: Cloudflare's DEFAULT 'Automatic' placement was accepted unchanged. The creation screen stated: 'We have chosen to place your bucket in Eastern North America.' No location hint was provided and no jurisdiction restriction was set.
bucketCreation.locationNote: This happens to differ from insite-production (WNAM), which is incidentally useful but is NOT claimed as an independent disaster-recovery guarantee — §311A forbade that inference and it would be unfounded. Both buckets are in the same Cloudflare account, and account-level loss is common-mode to both regardless of placement.
bucketCreation.storageClassReasoning: Standard was the default and is also the correct choice. Infrequent Access carries a minimum storage duration and retrieval charges; with 14-day daily retention, artifacts would routinely be deleted before that minimum and incur early-deletion charges. The cheaper-sounding class would have cost money.

tenPointVerification.1_bucketExists: YES — listed in R2 Object Storage, settings page loads, Objects tab reports 'Your bucket is ready.'
tenPointVerification.2_bucketPrivate: YES — bucket Objects view reports 'Public Access: Disabled'. The creation screen also stated 'By default buckets are not publicly accessible.'
tenPointVerification.3_publicDevelopmentUrlDisabled: YES — 'The public development URL is disabled for this bucket.'
tenPointVerification.4_noCustomDomain: YES — 'There is no custom domain assigned to this bucket.'
tenPointVerification.5_noCorsOrPublicExposure: YES — 'There is no CORS Policy defined for this bucket.' R2 Data Catalog disabled. On Demand Migration not enabled. Local Uploads disabled.

6_noUnexpectedLifecycleDeletion.interpretation: R2 applies this default housekeeping rule to every new bucket automatically; it was not configured by §311A. It discards INCOMPLETE MULTIPART UPLOADS after seven days and never deletes a completed object. insite-production carries the identical rule. No object-expiry rule exists on either bucket.

tenPointVerification.7_noUnexpectedLockRule: YES — 'There are no bucket lock rules defined for this bucket.' None was created; §311A forbade it.
tenPointVerification.8_locationPlacement: Eastern North America (ENAM), via Cloudflare's Automatic placement. Recorded above.

otherControls.clientIpFiltering: Include / Exclude lists available; default applies to all addresses

existingTokensUnchanged.significance: This confirms §311's inference from the 403 responses and sharpens it: the application credential is an OBJECT-level token scoped to a SINGLE bucket, which is why every bucket-administration call was denied. It also means the application credential has NO access whatsoever to insite-backups — the isolation §311 asked for exists by construction the moment the new bucket was created, before any new token is minted.

recommendedMinimumPermissions.appliedTo: Apply to specific buckets only -> insite-backups

why.writeNeeded: PutObject for the dump, its metadata sidecar and latest.json
why.readNeeded: GetObject for the mandatory post-upload read-back-and-re-hash, and for downloading the artifact during a restore
why.deleteIsIncludedEvidence: Object Read & Write covers delete. Established empirically rather than assumed: the application token is Object Read & Write and its tombstone and retireReportArtifact paths successfully delete objects in production today.

recommendedMinimumPermissions.whyNotAdmin: Admin Read & Write would let this credential DELETE THE BACKUP BUCKET ITSELF and edit bucket configuration. A backup credential that can destroy the backup destination inverts the control it exists to provide. Nothing in the mechanism needs bucket-level operations.
recommendedMinimumPermissions.whyNotObjectReadOnly: Retention must delete expired artifacts and the backup must write; read-only cannot do either.

ttlRecommendation.reasoning: A finite TTL is better hygiene, but an expiring credential makes backups start failing silently on a date nobody remembers. The mitigation exists — the freshness monitor returns UNKNOWN and alerts when it cannot authenticate — so the failure would be caught rather than silent. For Beta the simpler option is chosen deliberately, and credential rotation is recorded as future hardening rather than pretended away.

ipFilteringRecommendation.reasoning: It sounds like free defence and is not. The backup runs from the owner's laptop on a residential and therefore dynamic address, and from different networks when travelling. An IP filter would convert an ordinary network change into a silent backup outage. The credential's real containment is that it is object-scoped to one operator-only bucket.
